aspects.says: cancel(true) on a RecursiveTask has the same effect as cancel(false): it marks a task that isn't done as cancelled and interrupts nothing, so a running task runs to its end.
basis: section:A Subtask's Exception Reaches join() as a Copy, and Its Siblings Keep Running

aspects.says: The value a task returns must hold enough to combine with its sibling's so that any split gives the answer one task would: sets for a distinct count, sum and count for an average, every value's count for the most frequent one.
basis: section:The Parent Can Only Combine What Its Halves Return

aspects.says: A subtask's exception reaches a joining thread on another thread as a new exception of the same class with the original as its cause, one copy per thread crossed, so its message can be null or prefixed; the original is found by following getCause() while it is the same class.
basis: section:A Subtask's Exception Reaches join() as a Copy, and Its Siblings Keep Running

aspects.says: Each task returns its part of the answer and the parent combines the values it joins; leaves that write into shared state lose updates, and a thread-safe field held by the object that runs the task still mixes the totals of two runs.
basis: section:A Task Returns Its Part of the Answer; Tasks That Write into Shared State Lose It

aspects.says: A failure doesn't stop the other subtasks: forked halves that were never joined still run, so tasks that should stop after a failure check a flag that the failing task sets.
basis: section:A Subtask's Exception Reaches join() as a Copy, and Its Siblings Keep Running

aspects.says: Splitting shares work among workers but can't remove work a recursion repeats: recursive Fibonacci as tasks is at best the number of workers faster than one thread, and a task per call is slower than one thread, while a loop does a few additions.
basis: section:Splitting Shares the Work Among Workers; It Can't Remove Work the Recursion Repeats
